episodes.summary_en: Hoya spends Seollal, the Lunar New Year, with a family: new seolbim clothes, a New Year bow (sebae), a warm bowl of tteokguk, and a lively game of yunnori.
learning_goals: Explain that Seollal is the first day of the first lunar month and one of Korea's biggest traditional holidays.
Recognize and say 설날, 세배, 떡국 and 윷놀이, and the greeting 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
Describe sebae (the New Year bow) and deokdam (words of blessing from elders).
Name the five yut throws (do, gae, geol, yut, mo) and how many spaces each one moves.

scenes.narration_en: Good morning! I'm Hoya. Today is Seollal, the Lunar New Year. It falls on the first day of the first month of the lunar calendar, and it is one of Korea's biggest traditional holidays.
scenes.illustration: Hoya the young tiger waving at the gate of a traditional hanok house on a crisp winter morning, a pale sunrise over snowy roof tiles.

scenes.narration_en: People dress in new clothes for the new year. New Seollal clothes are called seolbim. Young girls traditionally wear saekdong jeogori, a jacket with rainbow-striped sleeves.
scenes.illustration: A family in bright hanbok; a girl spreads her arms to show rainbow-striped saekdong sleeves while Hoya admires them.

scenes.narration_en: After the morning rites for the family's ancestors, the children bow deeply to Grandma and Grandpa. This New Year bow is called sebae, the first greeting of the year.
scenes.illustration: Two children bowing deeply on a heated wooden floor before smiling grandparents seated on cushions; Hoya bows beside them.

scenes.narration_en: After bowing, Hoya says, 'Saehae bok mani badeuseyo!' Grandma answers with kind wishes for the year, called deokdam. Children may get a little money, or rice cakes and fruit.
scenes.gloss_en: Happy New Year! (literally: Receive many blessings in the new year)
scenes.illustration: Grandma smiling and handing a small envelope to a child; a plate of rice cakes and tangerines on a low table; Hoya beaming.

scenes.narration_en: Breakfast is tteokguk: a clear soup with thin slices of white rice cake. People have long said that you grow one year older when you eat your bowl of tteokguk on Seollal!
scenes.illustration: Steaming bowls of clear soup with oval white rice-cake slices and egg garnish on a low table; Hoya holding a spoon happily.

scenes.narration_en: Now for a game of yunnori! Two teams take turns throwing four wooden yut sticks. Depending on how the sticks land, a team moves its pieces around the board.
scenes.illustration: Four wooden yut sticks tumbling in mid-air above a cloth game board with a circle-and-cross pattern; two teams cheering, Hoya on one team.

scenes.narration_en: Do moves one space, gae two, geol three, yut four, and mo five! Throw a yut or a mo and you throw again. The first team to bring all its pieces home wins.
scenes.illustration: Five small panels in a row showing yut sticks landing in five different patterns, each with a matching number of footprints (1 to 5), no letters.

scenes.narration_en: In 2023, Korea named five traditional holidays, including Seol and Daeboreum (New Year through the first full moon), as National Intangible Heritage. Yunnori was named in 2022. Hoya bows: 'Saehae bok mani badeuseyo!'
scenes.illustration: Night scene of a big round full moon over a village, with Hoya bowing toward the viewer and a yut board resting nearby.

facts.claim_en: Seollal (Seol) is the first day of the first month of the lunar calendar and one of Korea's major traditional holidays; in the late Joseon era the book Dongguk sesigi counted Seol, Hansik, Dano and Chuseok as the four great holidays.
facts.claim_ko: 설(설날)은 음력 정월 초하루로 우리나라의 대표 명절이며, 조선 후기 『동국세시기』는 설·한식·단오·추석을 4대 명절로 꼽았다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 설과 대보름 (The Traditional Holidays of Seol and Daeboreum)
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘설과 대보름은 음력 정월 초하루에서 보름까지 해당하며, 한 해의 시작을 기념하는 인류 보편적 ‘신년맞이 명절’이다.’ / ‘조선시대 설은 중종 13년(1518년) 단오·추석과 함께 3대 명절로 꼽았고, 조선 후기 간행된 『동국세시기』에 따르면 한식·단오·추석과 더불어 4대 명절로 손꼽았다.’

sources.title: 설
sources.quote_or_locator: 정의: ‘한 해의 시작인 음력 1월 1일을 일컫는 말로 설날이라는 말과 같은 우리나라의 명절.’ / ‘조선시대는 원단·한식·단오·추석을 4대 명절이라 했지만’

facts.claim_en: New clothes for Seollal are called seolbim; young girls in particular traditionally wear saekdong jeogori (a jacket with rainbow-striped sleeves).
facts.claim_ko: 설을 맞아 새로 장만해 입는 옷을 설빔이라 하며, 특히 여자 어린이들은 색동저고리를 입는다.

sources.title: 설
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘설날에 입는 옷을 설빔이라 한다.’ … ‘설날에 색깔이 있는 옷을 입는데 특히 여자 어린이들은 색동저고리를 입는다.’

sources.title: 설빔
sources.publisher: 국립국어원 (National Institute of Korean Language) — 표준국어대사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘설을 맞이하여 새로 장만하여 입거나 신는 옷, 신발 따위를 이르는 말.’

facts.claim_en: Sebae is the New Year bow to elders, the first greeting of the year; after the ancestral rites (charye), children bow first to grandparents and parents.
facts.claim_ko: 세배는 정월 초하룻날 윗사람에게 절을 하는 새해의 첫인사로, 차례를 지낸 뒤 조부모·부모에게 먼저 절한다.

sources.title: 세배
sources.quote_or_locator: 정의: ‘정월 초하룻날 윗사람에게 절을 하는 새해의 첫인사.’ 내용: ‘차례를 지낸 뒤에 자리를 정리하여 앉는다. 그리고는 조부모·부모에게 먼저 절하고’

sources.title: 국가무형유산 설과 대보름
sources.quote_or_locator: English description: ‘Seol customs such as observing ancestral rites at home (charye), bowing to elder kin (sebae), and eating a bowl of tteokguk’

facts.claim_en: When bowing, people say New Year wishes such as “Saehae bok mani badeuseyo” (Receive lots of blessings in the new year); this greeting is a modern-era form of New Year wish.
facts.claim_ko: 세배 때 ‘새해 복 많이 받으세요’와 같은 새해 인사말을 하며, 이 인사말은 현대에 널리 쓰이게 된 덕담이다.

sources.title: 세배
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘웃어른에게 세배를 할 때는 절을 하고 나서 “새해에는 더욱 건강하시기를 빕니다.”, “새해에는 복 많이 받으시고 오래오래 사십시오.” 등의 새해 인사말을 한다.’

sources.title: 설
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘실상 “새해 복 많이 받으십시오”라는 신년 인사말은 전통적인 덕담이 아니라 새로 생긴 현대판 덕담이다.’

facts.claim_en: Elders who receive sebae answer with words of blessing (deokdam); children who come to bow are given a little money, or rice cakes and fruit.
facts.claim_ko: 세배를 받는 어른은 덕담을 하고, 아이들에게는 약간의 돈 또는 떡과 과일을 준다.

sources.title: 세배
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘세배를 받는 이도 … 한마디씩 덕담을 한다.’ / ‘아이들에게는 술은 주지 않고 약간의 돈, 또는 떡과 과일을 준다.’

sources.title: 덕담
sources.publisher: 국립국어원 (National Institute of Korean Language) — 표준국어대사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘남이 잘되기를 비는 말. 주로 새해에 많이 나누는 말이다.’

facts.claim_en: Tteokguk, a clear broth with thinly sliced white rice cake (garaetteok), is the representative Seollal food, and there is a long-standing saying that you become one year older by eating tteokguk.
facts.claim_ko: 떡국은 맑은 장국에 가래떡을 얇게 썰어 넣고 끓인 설날 음식이며, 떡국을 먹어야 나이 한 살을 먹는다는 말이 전한다.

sources.title: 떡국
sources.quote_or_locator: 정의: ‘맑은 장국에 가래떡을 얇게 썰어넣고 끓인 음식.’ 내용: ‘설날에 먹는 절식(節食)의 하나이다.’

sources.title: 설
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘세찬의 대표적인 음식인 떡국을 먹어야 나이 한 살을 먹는다고 했다.’

sources.title: 국가무형유산 설과 대보름
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘설의 핵심 요소인 설 차례, 새배, 떡국을 먹는 풍속이 확인된다.’ (원문 표기 그대로)

sources.title: 떡국 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘멥쌀을 가루내어 떡메로 친 후, 손으로 길게 만든 흰 가래떡을 썰어서 맑은 장국에 넣고 끓인 음식으로 정조차례(正朝茶禮)시에 세찬(歲饌)으로 먹는 시절음식.’

facts.claim_en: In yunnori (yut game) two sides take turns throwing four wooden yut sticks; depending on how the sticks land, they move their pieces on the board, and the side that first brings all its pieces to the goal wins. It is played from New Year's Day to Jeongwol Daeboreum.
facts.claim_ko: 윷놀이는 양편으로 나뉘어 윷가락 4개를 던져, 엎어지고 젖혀진 상태에 따라 윷판의 모든 말을 목적지에 먼저 도달시키는 편이 이기는 놀이로, 정초부터 정월대보름까지 즐긴다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 윷놀이 (Yut nori)
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘‘윷놀이’는 양편으로 나뉘어 윷가락 4개를 던져, 윷가락이 엎어지고 젖혀진 상태에 따라 윷판의 모든 말을 목적지에 먼저 도달시키는 편이 이기는 놀이로, 정초(正初)부터 정월대보름까지 …’

sources.title: ‘윷놀이’ 무형문화재 됐다…“민족 정체성 담은 전통 놀이” (2022.11.11)
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘윷놀이는 윷가락 4개를 던져 윷판의 모든 말을 목적지에 먼저 도달시키는 편이 이기는 놀이로’

sources.title: 윷놀이
sources.quote_or_locator: 정의: ‘정월 초하루부터 대보름까지 즐기며, 4개의 윷가락을 던지고 그 결과에 따라 말[馬]을 사용하여 승부를 겨루는 민속놀이.’

facts.claim_en: The five throws move a piece as follows: do 1 space, gae 2, geol 3, yut 4, mo 5; throwing yut or mo earns another throw.
facts.claim_ko: 도는 한 발, 개는 두 발, 걸은 세 발, 윷은 네 발, 모는 다섯 발을 가며, 윷이나 모가 나오면 한 번 더 던진다.

sources.title: 윷놀이
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘도는 한 발, 개는 두 발, 걸은 세 발, 윷은 네 발, 모는 다섯 발을 간다.’ / ‘모나 윷이 나오면 한번 더 할 수가 있으며’

sources.title: 도 / 개 / 걸 / 모 (표제어)
sources.publisher: 국립국어원 (National Institute of Korean Language) — 표준국어대사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘모’: ‘윷놀이에서, 윷짝의 네 개가 다 엎어진 경우를 이르는 말. 끗수는 다섯 끗으로 친다.’ (같은 사전 ‘도’ 한 끗, ‘개’ 두 끗, ‘걸’ 세 끗)

facts.claim_en: On 18 December 2023, Korea designated five traditional holidays — Seol and Daeboreum, Hansik, Dano, Chuseok and Dongji — as National Intangible Heritage. Daeboreum (the 15th day of the first lunar month) celebrates the first full moon after the Lunar New Year.
facts.claim_ko: 2023년 12월 18일 ‘설과 대보름’, ‘한식’, ‘단오’, ‘추석’, ‘동지’ 5개 명절이 국가무형유산으로 지정되었다. 정월대보름(음력 1월 15일)은 새해 첫 보름달을 맞는 명절이다.

sources.title: 5개 명절(설과 대보름, 한식, 단오, 추석, 동지) 국가무형유산 신규종목 지정 (2023-12-18)
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘문화재청(청장 최응천)은 우리 민족의 5개 대표 명절 ‘설과 대보름’, ‘한식’, ‘단오’, ‘추석’, ‘동지’를 신규 국가무형유산으로 지정한다.’

sources.title: 설·대보름 등 우리 민족 5대 명절, 국가무형유산으로 지정 (2023.12.18)
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘문화재청은 18일 우리 민족의 5개 대표 명절 설과 대보름, 한식, 단오, 추석, 동지를 신규 국가무형유산으로 지정한다고 밝혔다.’

episodes.notes: Romanization: 윷놀이 is pronounced [윤노리], so RR gives 'yunnori'; the Korea Heritage Service's English name is 'Yut nori' and the app's existing card uses 'yutnori'. Pick one spelling app-wide. 'Saehae bok mani badeuseyo' is the greeting most people use today, but the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture calls it a modern greeting (older ones include '과세 안녕히 하셨습니까'). The narration keeps that in facts and doesn't call it ancient. The tteokguk age saying is presented only as a saying. Sebae money (세뱃돈) is described the way the Encyclopedia does: 'a little money, or rice cakes and fruit'. Left out on purpose: the sources don't explain which way up the yut sticks count for each throw (엎어지다/젖혀지다), so the narration doesn't say. Also left out are 차례 table details, 복조리, and 안택 rites. Note for existing content: heritage-cards.ts says tteokguk slices 'look like coins for good luck'. None of the sources checked here supports that, so it's not used here; please review it. REVISION 2026-10-10: "four great holidays" now stated as the late-Joseon Dongguk sesigi listing (the 1518 list had three: Seol, Dano, Chuseok, per the KHS portal). Check 3 reworded to an in-story question; "Everyone" softened to "People".

episodes.title_en: Dano Day: Swings, Masks and Ssireum
episodes.summary_en: Hoya celebrates Dano, Korea's early-summer holiday: hair washed in changpo water, high-flying swings, ssireum wrestling, and the UNESCO-listed Gangneung Danoje with its wordless Gwanno mask drama.
learning_goals: Say when Dano falls (5th day of the 5th lunar month) and name two Dano customs (changpo hair-washing, swinging).
Describe how ssireum is won and what jangsa means.
Explain that Gangneung Danoje (proclaimed 2005, inscribed 2008) and ssireum (2018, joint inscription by both Koreas) are on UNESCO's Representative List.
Recognize and say 단오, 그네, 씨름, 장사 and 탈.

scenes.narration_en: Summer is almost here! Today is Dano, the fifth day of the fifth lunar month. A late-Joseon book, Dongguk sesigi, counted it among Korea's four great holidays, with lots of games and fun.
scenes.gloss_en: Dano (5th day of the 5th lunar month)
scenes.illustration: Hoya in a light summer hanbok on a green hillside in early summer, rice paddies freshly planted below.

scenes.narration_en: Long ago on Dano, people washed their hair in water boiled with changpo, a fragrant plant called sweet flag. They said it made hair thick and shiny.
scenes.illustration: Women by a stream rinsing long hair in a wooden basin; tall sword-shaped sweet-flag leaves at the water's edge; Hoya sniffing a leaf.

scenes.narration_en: Swings hang from tall trees, and people soar into the sky! Swinging, called geunettwigi, has been a favorite Dano game since long ago.
scenes.illustration: A person in hanbok standing on a long rope swing hung from a big old tree, flying high; Hoya cheering below.

scenes.narration_en: Another Dano favorite is ssireum, Korean wrestling. Two wrestlers grip each other's satba, a cloth belt around the waist and thigh. In a modern match, whoever first touches the ground with any part of the body from the knee up loses!
scenes.illustration: Two wrestlers crouched shoulder to shoulder in a sand ring, each gripping the other's cloth thigh belt; Hoya as a referee.

scenes.narration_en: The champion is called jangsa, meaning 'a very strong person.' Traditionally the winner received an ox, a symbol of plenty in a farming village!
scenes.illustration: A smiling champion riding a calm brown ox around the sand ring while villagers clap; Hoya leading the ox by a rope.

scenes.narration_en: On Korea's east coast, the city of Gangneung holds a big Dano festival: Gangneung Danoje. It begins with brewing a special drink for the gods, and people hold rites praying for a peaceful village and good harvests.
scenes.illustration: A riverside festival ground with colorful paper lanterns and banners, a ritual table with offerings, mountains in the distance; Hoya in the crowd.

scenes.narration_en: Look, masks! In the Gwanno mask drama, performers make the audience laugh using only gestures. They never say a word! It is known as Korea's only mask drama with no spoken lines.
scenes.illustration: Masked performers in a playful pose on an open-air stage: a long-bearded nobleman (yangban) mask and a white-faced young-lady (somae-gaksi) mask; the audience laughing, Hoya giggling.

scenes.narration_en: In 2005, UNESCO proclaimed Gangneung Danoje a masterpiece of intangible heritage; in 2008 it joined the Representative List. In 2018, ssireum was inscribed after North and South Korea merged their applications, which UNESCO called unprecedented.
scenes.illustration: Hoya holding a glowing heritage card with a swing, a mask and two wrestlers on it, standing under festival lanterns.

facts.claim_en: Dano falls on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month and is a representative summer holiday rich in games and customs. In 1518 it was counted among three great holidays (with Seollal and Chuseok); in the late Joseon era the book Dongguk sesigi counted it among four (Seol, Hansik, Dano, Chuseok).

episodes.notes: Left out on purpose: the story that Dano comes from China (Qu Yuan), folk etymology of 수릿날, the 석전 (stone fight) custom, shamanic (굿) details, the festival's deities by name (김유신, 범일국사, 정씨 처녀), and how long the festival lasts. Sources describe its length differently (UNESCO says four weeks; the 국가유산포털 says 5 days of rites at the 단오장). The 'only silent mask drama' claim comes from one official source (국가유산청 국가유산포털), so the narration hedges it as 'known as'. The knee rule describes modern competition ssireum (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture). The narration uses 'east coast' and doesn't name the sea. 단오 was also designated National Intangible Heritage on 2023-12-18. That's covered in the Seollal episode and not repeated here. The 2023 Dano designation (KHS press release) is available if wanted. Standard spelling note: 단옷날 (with 사이시옷) is the dictionary form; the title uses 단오 only. UNESCO: Danoje proclaimed 2005, inscribed 2008 (stated both). Ox: UNESCO says ox; encykorea says 황소 (bull) - narration follows UNESCO. episodes.title_en: Chuseok: Songpyeon Under the Full Moon
episodes.summary_en: At Chuseok (Hangawi), Hoya joins a family going back to their hometown, makes songpyeon steamed on pine needles, and watches women dance Ganggangsullae hand in hand under the full moon.
learning_goals: Say when Chuseok falls (15th day of the 8th lunar month) and that its native name is Hangawi.
Describe songpyeon and how they are made (fillings; steamed on pine needles).
Describe Ganggangsullae (women in a circle, call-and-response singing) and that UNESCO inscribed it in 2009.
Recognize and say 추석, 한가위, 송편, 보름달 and 강강술래.

scenes.narration_en: It's Chuseok, also called Hangawi! It falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, just as the harvest begins. Families give thanks for the year's crops.
scenes.illustration: Golden rice fields under an autumn sky, persimmon trees heavy with orange fruit; Hoya stretching happily at the edge of the field.

scenes.narration_en: Many people travel back to their hometowns. In the morning, families honor their ancestors with a table of food, called charye, and then visit their ancestors' graves, called seongmyo.
scenes.illustration: A family in hanbok standing respectfully before a low table set with fruit and dishes; later a grassy hillside path; Hoya walking quietly with them.

scenes.narration_en: The night before, under the bright moon, the family makes songpyeon together. They wrap rice dough around fillings like sesame, beans or chestnuts. Rice from the new harvest makes them extra tasty!
scenes.gloss_en: small filled rice cakes for Chuseok
scenes.illustration: Family members around a low table shaping small white, green and pink rice cakes; bowls of sesame, beans and chestnuts; Hoya pinching one closed.

scenes.narration_en: Shaped like little half-moons, the songpyeon are steamed on a bed of pine needles. Mmm, smell the fresh pine! Hoya tries one. Yum!
scenes.illustration: A bamboo steamer opened to reveal glossy rice cakes resting on green pine needles, wisps of steam; Hoya sniffing with closed eyes.

scenes.narration_en: That night, a big round full moon rises. In old farming villages the full moon meant plenty, and Chuseok was even called 'the holiday of the moon.'
scenes.illustration: A huge glowing full moon rising over a quiet village of thatched and tiled roofs; Hoya sitting on a stone wall gazing up.

scenes.narration_en: Under the moon, women join hands in a circle for Ganggangsullae. A lead singer calls out a line, and everyone answers, 'Ganggangsullae!' The song starts slow, then gets faster and faster until they are almost running.
scenes.illustration: Women in hanbok holding hands in a wide circle on a moonlit field, skirts swirling, one singer at the front; Hoya clapping along outside the circle.

scenes.narration_en: Between dances they play games with fun names, like 'bracken picking' and 'herring tying.' The dance has long been done along Korea's southwestern coast. And no one knows exactly what the word 'ganggangsullae' means!
scenes.illustration: Dancers crouched in a line like ferns while a leader 'picks' them one by one; a coastline with small islands in the moonlight behind; Hoya scratching his head curiously.

scenes.narration_en: In 2009, UNESCO inscribed Ganggangsullae on its Representative List. The Joseon-era book Yeoryang sesigi records an old saying like this: 'No more, no less, may it always be like Hangawi!'
scenes.korean: 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라
scenes.romanization: Deodo malgo deoldo malgo hangawiman gatara
scenes.gloss_en: No more, no less: may it always be like Hangawi. (the familiar modern wording)
scenes.illustration: Hoya and the family sharing songpyeon and fruit on a wooden porch under the full moon, the dance circle glowing in the distance.

facts.claim_en: On the evening before Chuseok (the 14th), families gather under the bright moon to make songpyeon, rice-dough cakes filled with fillings such as beans, sesame or chestnuts; made from newly harvested grain, they taste especially good.
facts.claim_ko: 추석 전날(열나흗날) 저녁 밝은 달을 보며 가족이 모여 콩·깨·밤 등을 소로 넣은 송편을 빚으며, 햇곡식으로 만들어 더욱 맛이 있다.

sources.title: 추석
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘열 나흗날 저녁 밝은 달을 보면서 가족들이 모여 송편을 만든다.’ / ‘송편 속에도 콩 · 팥 · 밤 · 대추 등을 넣는데, 모두 햇것으로 한다. 모두 햇곡식이기 때문에 더욱 맛이 있다.’

sources.title: 송편
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘팔월 추석에는 햅쌀로 송편을 빚어 차례를 지내고’ / ‘팥송편·깨송편·대추송편·잣송편’

facts.claim_en: Songpyeon are often shaped like a half-moon and are steamed on a layer of pine needles; the scent of pine is said to make the rice cake taste better.
facts.claim_ko: 송편은 흔히 반달 모양으로 빚어 솔잎을 깔고 찌며, 솔잎의 소나무 향이 떡의 맛을 좋게 한다고 한다.

sources.title: 송편
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 어린이민속사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘송편은 멥쌀가루 반죽에 팥, 콩, 밤, 대추, 깨 등을 넣고 반달이나 모시조개 모양으로 만들어서 솔잎을 깔고 찐 떡입니다. … 솔잎에서 나오는 소나무 향은 떡의 맛을 좋게 합니다.’

sources.title: 송편 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘멥쌀가루를 익반죽하고 풋콩, 깨, 밤 같은 소를 넣어 반달 모양으로 빚어서 시루에 솔잎을 켜켜로 놓고 찐 떡.’

sources.title: 송편 (미디어 설명)
sources.quote_or_locator: 미디어 캡션: ‘멥쌀가루를 뜨거운 물로 반죽하여 소를 넣고 모양을 만들어 솔잎을 깔고 찐 떡이다. 추석에 먹는 음식이다.’

facts.claim_en: In traditional farming life the Chuseok full moon was a symbol of plenty, and Chuseok was even called 'the holiday of the moon'.
facts.claim_ko: 전통 농경사회에서 추석 보름달은 풍요를 상징했으며, 추석을 ‘달의 명절’이라 부르기도 했다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 추석
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘The full moon on Chuseok is understood as a symbol of prosperity, fecundity, and a bountiful crop.’ / ‘추석을 ‘달의 명절’이라 이르기도 하였다.’

facts.claim_en: In Ganggangsullae, performed on moonlit nights around Chuseok, women join hands and move in a circle; a lead singer sings a line and the others answer 'Ganggangsullae', and the song and dance start slow and grow faster until the dancers are almost running.
facts.claim_ko: 강강술래는 추석 무렵 달밤에 여인들이 손에 손을 잡고 원을 그리며, 앞소리꾼이 메기면 나머지가 ‘강강술래’로 받는다. 처음엔 느리다가 점점 빨라져 나중에는 뛰는 듯하다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 강강술래 (Ganggangsullae)
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘여인들은 손에 손을 잡고 오른쪽으로 돌며 둥근 원을 그려나간다. 목청 좋고 소리 잘하는 사람이 맨 앞에 서서 메기는 소리를 하면 나머지 사람들은 ‘강강술래’하며 받는 소리를 한다. 처음에는 늦은 가락으로 나아가다 … 나중에는 뛰는 것처럼 동작이 빨라진다.’

sources.title: Ganggangsullae
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘Under a bright full moon, dozens of young, unmarried village women gather in a circle, join hands’ / ‘sing and dance all night under the direction of a lead singer.’

sources.title: 강강술래 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘동산에 보름달이 떠오르면 마을의 넓은 마당으로 모인 여자들이 느린 가락에 맞춰 늦은강강술래를 추다가 흥이 점점 더해감에 따라 속도가 빨라져서 마침내 잦은강강술래로 이어진다.’ / ‘한 사람이 설소리(앞소리)를 하면, 나머지 사람이 매김소리(뒷소리)를 받는’

facts.claim_en: Ganggangsullae includes accompanying folk games such as 'bracken picking' (gosari-kkeokgi) and 'herring tying' (cheongeo-yeokgi).
facts.claim_ko: 강강술래에는 고사리꺾기, 청어엮기 등의 놀이가 곁들여진다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 강강술래
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘남생이놀이를 비롯해서 고사리꺾기, 청어엮기, 기와밟기, 꼬리따기 …’ / English: ‘folk games such as “bracken picking,” “herring tying,” “tile treading,”’

sources.title: 고사리타령
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘고사리꺾기 놀이는 강강술래 여흥 놀이의 하나로도 포함되어 있으나 독립적인 놀이로도 행해졌다.’

sources.title: 강강술래 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘남생이놀이, 고사리꺾기, 청어엮기, 지와밟기, 꼬리따기, 덕석말이 … 같은 여성들이 하는 놀이’

facts.claim_en: Ganggangsullae has traditionally been performed mainly along the southwestern coast of Korea (the coast of Jeollanam-do). Its exact origin is uncertain; the Korea Heritage Service considers an origin in ancient moonlit-night festivals more plausible than the popular Admiral Yi Sun-sin story.
facts.claim_ko: 강강술래는 전통적으로 주로 한반도 서남 해안 지방(전라남도 해안)에서 행해졌다. 정확한 기원은 확실하지 않으며, 국가유산청은 이순신 장군 유래설보다 달 밝은 밤의 고대 축제에서 비롯되었다고 보는 것이 타당하다고 설명한다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 강강술래
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘주로 전라남도 해안지방에서 추석을 전후하여 달밤에 행해졌다.’ / ‘임진왜란 때 이순신 장군이 … 비롯되었다는 설이 있으나, 원시시대부터 1년중 가장 달이 밝은 밤에 축제를 벌여 노래하고 춤추던 풍습에서 비롯된 민속놀이라고 보는 것이 타당하다.’

sources.title: Ganggangsullae
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘a seasonal harvest and fertility ritual popular in the south-western part of the Republic of Korea’

sources.title: 강강술래
sources.quote_or_locator: 정의: ‘추석날 밤이나 정월 대보름날 밤에 … 서남 해안지방에서 행하는 노래와 무용과 놀이가 혼합된 성인여자놀이.’

sources.title: 강강술래 (한국세시풍속사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘강강술래의 유래는 확실하지 않다.’ / ‘전승 지역으로 보면 호남 일원이요, 연행 시기로 보면 8월 한가위가 일반적이며, 연행 주체는 주로 마을의 여자들이다.’

facts.claim_en: The dance is named after its refrain, but the exact meaning of the word 'ganggangsullae' is unknown.
facts.claim_ko: 강강술래라는 이름은 후렴에서 왔지만 그 말의 정확한 뜻은 알려져 있지 않다.

sources.title: Ganggangsullae
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘The dance takes its name from the refrain repeated after each verse, although the exact meaning of the word is unknown.’

facts.claim_en: Ganggangsullae was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009.
facts.claim_ko: 강강술래는 2009년 유네스코 인류무형문화유산 대표목록에 등재되었다.

sources.title: Ganggangsullae
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘Inscribed in 2009 (4.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity’

facts.claim_en: The Joseon-era book Yeoryang sesigi (by Gim Mae-sun) records people saying, in Chinese characters, 'No more, no less, may it always be like Hangawi'; the familiar modern Korean wording is 'Deodo malgo deoldo malgo hangawiman gatara'.
facts.claim_ko: 조선시대 김매순의 『열양세시기(洌陽歲時記)』에는 ‘더도 말고 덜도 말고 늘 한가위 같기만 바란다’는 뜻의 말이 한자로 실려 있으며, 오늘날 널리 쓰이는 표현은 “더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라”이다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 추석
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘조선시대 『열양세시기(冽陽歲時記)』에는 4대 명절이었던 추석을 중히 여겨 … 이런 의미로 “더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라”는 말이 수록되어 있다.’ (KHS gives the modern wording; the Hanja form is in the Folk Encyclopedia entry below)

sources.title: 더도 말고 덜도 말고 늘 가윗날만 같아라 (한국세시풍속사전)

sources.quote_or_locator: ‘김매순(金邁淳)의 『열양세시기(冽陽歲時記)』 8월 중추(中秋)에 보면 … 그래서 말하기를 ‘더도 말고 덜도 말고 늘 한가위 같기만 바란다(加也勿 減夜勿 但願長似嘉俳日)’라고 한다.’라고 기록되어 있다.’ (the dictionary prints 減夜勿)

episodes.notes: Left out on purpose: the popular claim that Ganggangsullae began as Admiral Yi Sun-sin's military trick. The 국가유산포털 mentions it only as one theory and says an origin in ancient moonlit-night festivals is more plausible, so it isn't used. Also left out are folk etymologies of 'ganggangsullae' (UNESCO says the meaning is unknown), songpyeon fortune-telling beliefs (spouse looks, pregnancy divination), and specific 차례 table rules. Songpyeon shape symbolism (half-moon) isn't claimed because the sources don't support it. The 국가유산포털 actually links songpyeon to the full moon in general terms. The existing heritage-cards.ts text 'half-moon rice cakes' and 'steamed on pine needles for fragrance' is only partly supported: pine-needle steaming is supported, but the shape and fragrance claims weren't verified. UNESCO describes the original dancers as young unmarried village women; today mostly middle-aged women in cities keep it alive. The narration says 'women'. 'Tile treading' was skipped because explaining it (walking on bent backs) needs care for young children. REVISION 2026-10-10: "comes from the southwest coast" -> "has long been done along the southwestern coast" (origin is uncertain per KHS and 한국세시풍속사전). Yeoryang sesigi saying: verified in the text quoted by 한국세시풍속사전 (Gim Mae-sun, 8th month entry; the Hanja there is printed 減夜勿, apparently a typo for 減也勿) - narration says the book "records an old saying like this" and gives the modern wording. Songpyeon: half-moon shape and pine scent are supported by the National Folk Museum (어린이민속사전; 한국세시풍속사전); the older note saying shape/fragrance were unverified is superseded. "warm and chewy" removed (not sourced).

episodes.title_en: Gimjang Day: Sharing Kimchi, Singing Arirang
episodes.summary_en: As winter comes, Hoya helps relatives and neighbors make and share kimchi for gimjang (UNESCO 2013), then hears Arirang, the folk song shared across Korea (South Korea's UNESCO entry, 2012).
learning_goals: Explain why families made gimjang kimchi and that sharing is at its heart.
Describe the yearly preparation for gimjang and the main ingredients (napa cabbage, chili powder, garlic, ginger, green onions).
Explain that Arirang is a folk song with many regional versions, and that UNESCO inscribed gimjang (2013) and South Korea's Arirang (2012); North Korea's Arirang has its own separate listing.
Recognize and say 김장, 김치, 배추, 고춧가루, 나눔 and 아리랑.

scenes.narration_en: Brrr! As late autumn turns to winter, Hoya visits a busy yard. Long ago, fresh vegetables were hard to find in winter, so families made lots of kimchi at once. This is gimjang (UNESCO spells it Kimjang).
scenes.illustration: A hanok courtyard in late autumn with bare trees, stacks of napa cabbages and big clay jars; Hoya in a warm vest arriving with a basket.

scenes.narration_en: Gimjang takes months of preparation! In spring, families get shrimp and anchovies for salting. In summer, they buy sea salt. In late summer, red chili peppers are dried and ground into chili powder.
scenes.illustration: Three small seasonal panels: spring jars of salted tiny shrimp, summer sacks of white sea salt, late-summer red chili peppers drying on mats in the sun.

scenes.narration_en: On gimjang day, relatives and neighbors come to help. They salt napa cabbages, then rub in a seasoning made with chili powder, garlic, ginger and green onions.
scenes.illustration: Neighbors in aprons and rubber gloves around big basins, rubbing red seasoning between cabbage leaves; garlic, ginger and green onions nearby; Hoya helping.

scenes.narration_en: Every region makes kimchi its own way. In the cold north it is often milder and less salty; in the south it is saltier, with a redder, richer seasoning. So there are countless kinds of kimchi!
scenes.illustration: A simple map-shaped table runner (no labels) with bowls of pale and deep-red kimchi placed from top to bottom; Hoya comparing two bowls.

scenes.narration_en: When the work is done, helpers often share boiled pork wrapped in the cabbage's yellow inner leaves. Many families give kimchi to neighbors, too. Working together and sharing are the heart of gimjang.
scenes.illustration: Helpers seated around a low table with sliced boiled pork and pale yellow cabbage leaves; a child carrying a covered dish of kimchi to the house next door; Hoya waving.

scenes.narration_en: In 2013, UNESCO inscribed 'Kimjang, making and sharing kimchi in the Republic of Korea' on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. In Korean, the Heritage Service calls it Gimchiwa gimjang munhwa.
scenes.gloss_en: Kimchi and Gimjang Culture (the Korean name of the UNESCO listing)
scenes.illustration: Rows of filled clay kimchi jars glowing in late-afternoon light, with Hoya proudly holding a heritage card showing cabbage and hands.

scenes.narration_en: As the day ends, Grandma hums a song known all over Korea: 'Arirang, arirang, arariyo…' Arirang is a folk song made and passed down by ordinary people over many generations.
scenes.illustration: Grandma resting on the wooden porch at dusk, humming with eyes closed, musical notes drifting toward mountain ridges; Hoya leaning on her shoulder.

scenes.narration_en: Arirang has many versions. Regions have their own, like Jeongseon, Jindo and Miryang Arirang, and anyone can make up new verses! UNESCO inscribed South Korea's Arirang in 2012. North Korea's Arirang has its own separate listing.
scenes.illustration: A winding mountain pass with three small scenes along it (mountain valley, island coast, river town), each with people singing; Hoya walking the path.

facts.claim_en: Because fresh vegetables were hard to get in winter, families made a large amount of kimchi at once in late autumn to early winter to last through the winter; this custom is gimjang (UNESCO: Kimjang).
facts.claim_ko: 겨울철에는 신선한 채소를 구하기 어려워 늦가을·초겨울에 겨우내 먹을 김치를 한꺼번에 많이 담갔으며, 이를 김장이라 한다.

sources.title: 김장
sources.quote_or_locator: 정의: ‘겨우내 먹을 김치를 한목에 담가두는 풍습.’ / ‘겨울철에는 신선한 채소를 구하기 어려웠으므로, 초겨울에 김치를 많이 담가서 저장하는 풍습이 발달하게 되었다.’

sources.title: Kimjang, making and sharing kimchi in the Republic of Korea
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘Late autumn is Kimjang season, when communities collectively make and share large quantities of kimchi’ … ‘to sustain it through the long, harsh winter.’

sources.title: 국가무형유산 김치 담그기 (Kimchi Making)
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘Kimchi making takes place on a large scale in early winter. This seasonal kimchi-making practice, or kimjang’

facts.claim_en: Gimjang preparation takes months (more than half a year, per the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture) and follows a yearly cycle: in spring households procure shrimp, anchovy and other seafood for salting, in summer they buy sea salt, and in late summer red chili peppers are dried and ground into powder.
facts.claim_ko: 김장 준비에는 반년 이상이 걸리며 1년 주기로 이어진다. 봄에는 새우·멸치 등 해산물을 구해 젓갈을 담그고, 여름에는 소금을 사며, 늦여름에는 고추를 말려 가루를 낸다.

sources.title: Kimjang, making and sharing kimchi in the Republic of Korea
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘Preparation follows a yearly cycle.’ / ‘In spring, households procure shrimp, anchovy and other seafood for salting and fermenting.’ / ‘In summer, they buy sea salt for the brine.’ / ‘In late summer, red chilli peppers are dried and ground into powder.’

sources.title: 김장
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘김장은 봄철의 젓갈담그기에서 초가을의 고추·마늘의 준비, 김장용 채소의 재배 등 준비하는 데에 반년 이상이 걸리는 한 가정의 큰 행사이었다.’

facts.claim_en: Relatives and neighbors help one another with gimjang: vegetables such as napa cabbage are salted, then mixed with a seasoning that includes chili powder, garlic, ginger and green onions.

episodes.reference_display: Sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage (Kimjang, 2013; Arirang in the Republic of Korea, 2012 - North Korea's Arirang is a separate 2014 entry); 국가유산청 국가유산포털(김치 담그기·아리랑·인류무형유산 목록); 한국민족문화대백과사전; 한국민속대백과사전(국립민속박물관)
episodes.notes: Spelling: RR for 김장/김치 is gimjang/gimchi. UNESCO's official title uses 'Kimjang', and 'kimchi' is the usual English word. The narration uses 'gimjang' (with UNESCO's spelling noted once) and 'kimchi'. Grandma humming Arirang at the end of the day is a story moment. The narration does not claim Arirang is a gimjang work song. The sources don't link the two, though some Arirang types are work songs (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture). The refrain quoted is the widely known one. The Encyclopedia notes the best-known 'Arirang' (경기/본조 아리랑) is a new folk-song (신민요) form; traditional regional ones include Jeongseon, Jindo and Miryang. Left out on purpose: UNESCO's estimate of 'some 3,600 variations'. Only one authoritative source for it was found, so it isn't in the narration. Also left out: theories about what 'Arirang' means (folk etymology), the DPRK listings (Arirang 2014; kimchi-making 2015), and the old practice of burying kimchi jars in the ground. National designations: 아리랑 (2015-09-22) and 김치 담그기 (2017-11-15) are National Intangible Heritage per the 국가유산포털. They aren't used in the narration. REVISION 2026-10-10: 'takes all year' -> 'takes months' (Encyclopedia: more than half a year; UNESCO: yearly cycle); 'sweet' and 'everyone' removed from scene 5; UNESCO title 'Kimjang, making and sharing kimchi in the Republic of Korea' (2013) and the Korea Heritage Service's Korean name 김치와 김장문화 now used; Arirang 2012 labelled South Korea's entry and the separate DPRK entry (2014) added as f10 (narration mentions 'separate listing' only; the 2014 year lives in f10); 'no exact translation' replaced by 'sung syllables' (encykorea: meaningless refrain, origin theories = folk etymology; 한국민속문학사전: 입타령 refrain).

episodes.title_en: The Sun and the Moon (A Traditional Tale)
episodes.summary_en: A gentle, simplified retelling of the traditional Korean folk tale Haenim Dallim: a brother and sister outwit a tricky tiger, climb a rope into the sky, and become the sun and the moon.
learning_goals: Recognize Haenim Dallim as a traditional Korean folk tale told in many versions, and this retelling as a simplified one.
Retell the main events: the tricky tiger, the tree, the rope from the sky, the sun and the moon.
Recognize and say 해, 달, 호랑이, 떡 and 동아줄.
Notice that folk tales sometimes 'explain' nature (why sorghum stalks are red) as part of the story, not as science.

scenes.narration_en: Story time with Hoya! This is an old Korean folk tale, told in many versions. It is called Haenim Dallim, The Sun and the Moon. Our retelling is simplified and gentler than the old tellings. And the tiger is a trickster, not like me!
scenes.gloss_en: the Sun and the Moon (with the respectful ending -nim; the tale's title)
scenes.illustration: Hoya sitting cross-legged with an open folding screen behind him painted with a sun, a moon and mountains, winking at the viewer.

scenes.narration_en: Long ago, a mother went out to work. Heading home with rice cakes, she met a tiger at a hill pass. 'Give me your rice cakes!' it said. The old tale has it ask for more at each hill. We keep it short.
scenes.illustration: A winding hilltop path at sunset; a mother in hanbok with a covered bundle of rice cakes, and a comical roly-poly tiger with no scary teeth peeking from behind a boulder; a thatched cottage far below.

scenes.narration_en: The tiger went to the children's house, pretending to be Mother. 'Open the door!' The children said, 'Your voice and hand are not Mother's!' But when the tiger said it must feed the crying baby, they opened the door.
scenes.illustration: A cottage door slightly ajar at dusk, two children peeking out with wide eyes; only a fuzzy striped paw and a shawl are visible outside, drawn comically rather than scary.

scenes.narration_en: Then the children realized it was the tiger, and they climbed a tall tree beside the well. Hoya whispers: 'Don't worry, it's only a story, and these two are clever!'
scenes.illustration: Two children perched high in a big tree beside a stone well under starlight, looking down calmly; a striped tail just visible behind the cottage; Hoya in a corner of the frame giving a thumbs-up.

scenes.narration_en: 'How did you get up there?' asked the tiger. The clever brother said, 'Rub on some sesame oil!' Slip, slide, bump! The tiger couldn't climb. But soon it found another way up.
scenes.illustration: The tiger sliding comically down a shiny tree trunk with a little oil bottle beside it, the children giggling behind their hands.

scenes.narration_en: The children prayed to the sky: 'Please send down a new rope!' A strong new rope came down, and up they climbed. The tiger tried a rope too, but it was old and rotten. Snap!
scenes.gloss_en: Please send down a new rope.
scenes.illustration: A thick golden rope descending from glowing clouds as the two children climb it; far below, a frayed grey rope snapping near the treetops.

scenes.narration_en: Down tumbled the tiger into a field of sorghum, and that was the end of its tricks. Storytellers say that is why sorghum stalks are red! The tale even has another name: 'Why Sorghum Stalks Are Red.'
scenes.illustration: A field of tall reddish sorghum stalks swaying, with only the tip of a striped tail sticking out among them; soft, funny mood.

scenes.narration_en: In the sky, the brother became the sun and the sister the moon. But she was scared of the dark night, so they swapped. Shy of people staring, the sister-sun shines so brightly that no one can look at her. They are safe and sound!
scenes.illustration: A split sky: a warm smiling sun with the sister's face on one side and a gentle moon with the brother's face on the other, over sleeping mountains; Hoya waving goodbye.

facts.claim_en: 'The Brother and Sister Who Became the Sun and the Moon' (also called Haenim Dallim) is a traditional Korean folk tale (mindam) told widely across the country, with many variant versions.
facts.claim_ko: 「해와 달이 된 오누이」(｢해님달님｣)는 전국적으로 널리 전승되는 민담이며 여러 변이형이 있다.

facts.claim_en: In the tale, a mother who has been out working meets a tiger on her way home. In the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture's basic version the tiger appears at one hill pass after another and makes demands in turn, rice cakes first and then more; this retelling keeps only the rice cakes and leaves out the rest.
facts.claim_ko: 이야기에서 품일을 나갔던 어머니가 돌아오는 길에 호랑이를 만난다. 대백과사전의 기본형에서는 호랑이가 고개마다 나타나 떡을 시작으로 차례로 여러 가지를 요구하는데, 이 재구성은 첫 번째인 떡만 남기고 나머지는 줄였다.

facts.claim_en: In the Encyclopedia's basic version, the tiger goes to the children's house pretending to be their mother; the children say the voice and hand are not their mother's and refuse to open the door, but open it when the tiger says it must nurse the crying baby; the siblings then realize who it is and flee up a big tree beside the well. Other versions differ (in the National Folk Museum's summary the children look through a hole in the door, see the tiger, and escape by the back door to a tree). This retelling is simplified.
facts.claim_ko: 대백과사전의 기본형에서 호랑이는 어머니인 척 아이들의 집에 찾아간다. 아이들은 목소리와 손바닥이 어머니와 다르다며 문을 열어 주지 않다가 호랑이가 우는 젖먹이에게 젖을 먹여야 한다고 하자 문을 열어 주고, 곧 호랑이의 정체를 알아차려 우물가 큰 나무 위로 피한다. 각편에 따라 다르며(국립민속박물관 줄거리에서는 문구멍으로 내다보고 호랑이인 줄 알아 뒷문으로 도망쳐 나무 위로 피한다), 이 재구성은 단순화한 것이다.

facts.claim_en: In the Encyclopedia's basic version, following the brother's advice the tiger rubs on sesame oil and fails to climb the tree, then finds another way up (the sister's advice).
facts.claim_ko: 대백과사전의 기본형에서 호랑이는 오빠의 말대로 참기름을 바르고 나무에 오르려다 실패하고, 이후 누이가 일러 준 다른 방법으로 올라간다.

sources.title: 해와 달이 된 오누이
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘처음에는 오빠의 말대로 참기름을 바르고 나무에 오르려다 실패하고, 그 다음에는 누이가 일러 준 대로 도끼로 나무를 찍으며 올라갔다.’ (the axe detail is left out of this retelling)

facts.claim_en: In the tale, the siblings pray to the sky for a rope; a new, strong rope (dongajul) comes down and they climb up, while the tiger takes a rotten rope that breaks.
facts.claim_ko: 남매가 하늘에 동아줄을 내려 달라고 빌자 새 동아줄이 내려와 하늘로 오르고, 호랑이가 잡은 썩은 동아줄은 끊어진다.

sources.title: 해와 달이 된 오누이
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘남매는 하늘에 동아줄을 내려 달라고 기원하여 하늘에서 내려온 새 동아줄을 타고 하늘로 올라갔고, 호랑이는 하늘에서 내려온 썩은 동아줄을 잡고 하늘로 오르다가 동아줄이 끊어져 수수밭에 떨어졌다.’

sources.title: 해와 달이 된 오누이 (한국민속문학사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: 줄거리: ‘오누이는 하늘에 빌어 하늘에서 내려준 쇠줄을 타고 올라가 … 호랑이도 오누이를 쫓아 썩은 동아줄을 타고 하늘에 오르다가 줄이 끊어져 …’ / 변이: ‘“살려주시려면 굵은 동아줄을, 죽이시려면 썩은 동아줄을 내려주세요.”라는 오누이의 기원’

sources.title: 동아줄
sources.publisher: 국립국어원 (National Institute of Korean Language) — 표준국어대사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘굵고 튼튼하게 꼰 줄.’

facts.claim_en: In the tale, the tiger falls from the rotten rope into a sorghum field, and storytellers use this to explain why sorghum stalks are red; some versions keep only the red-sorghum explanation, and the tale is also known as 'Why Sorghum Stalks Are Red'.
facts.claim_ko: 호랑이는 썩은 줄이 끊어져 수수밭에 떨어지고, 이야기는 이것으로 수숫대가 붉은 까닭을 설명한다. 수숫대가 붉어진 유래만 이야기하는 각편도 있으며, 이 설화는 ｢수숫대가 빨간 이유｣라고도 불린다.

sources.title: 해와 달이 된 오누이
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘동아줄이 끊어져 수수밭에 떨어졌다.’ / ‘수수가 붉게 되었다.’ / 개설: ‘｢수숫대가 빨간 이유｣라고도 부른다.’

sources.title: 해와 달이 된 오누이 (한국민속문학사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: 변이: ‘호랑이의 추락과 죽음으로 인해 수숫대가 붉어진 유래담도 형성되었다.’ / ‘해와 달에 관한 기원담은 생략되고 수숫대가 붉게 된 유래만 내용으로 삼는 유형도 있다.’

facts.claim_en: In the basic version, the brother first becomes the sun and the sister the moon, but because the sister is afraid of the night they swap. The sister, now the sun, is shy of people looking at her: the Encyclopedia says she pricks at people's eyes with needles so they cannot look straight at the sun, while the National Folk Museum's summary says she gives off a strong light. This retelling uses only the gentler 'too bright to look at' version. Versions differ (in some, the brother stays the sun).
facts.claim_ko: 기본형에서 오빠는 해, 누이는 달이 되었으나 누이가 밤을 무서워해 서로 바꾸었고, 해가 된 누이는 사람들이 쳐다보는 것이 부끄러워 사람들이 해를 똑바로 볼 수 없게 되었다. 대백과사전은 누이가 바늘로 눈을 콕콕 찌른다고 설명하고, 국립민속박물관 줄거리는 강력한 빛을 뿜는다고 설명하는데, 이 재구성은 순한 쪽(너무 밝아서 볼 수 없음)만 따랐다. 각편마다 다르다(오빠가 그대로 해가 되는 유형도 있다).

sources.title: 해와 달이 된 오누이
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘오빠는 해가 되고 누이는 달이 되었다. 그런데 누이가 밤이 무섭다고 하여 오빠가 바꿔 주어 누이는 해가 되고 오빠는 달이 되었다. 해가 된 누이는 낮에 사람들이 쳐다보는 것이 부끄러워 자신을 못 보게 바늘로 콕콕 찔러서 사람들이 해를 똑바로 쳐다볼 수 없게 되었다.’

sources.title: 해와 달이 된 오누이 (한국민속문학사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: 줄거리: ‘하느님이 오빠는 해, 동생은 달이 되게 하였지만 동생이 밤이 무섭다고 하여 역할을 바꾸어 오빠는 달, 여동생은 해가 된다. 여동생은 낮에 사람들이 쳐다보는 것이 부끄러워 강력한 빛을 뿜어낸다.’ / 변이: ‘누이가 무섭다고 해도 오빠가 한 번 정해진 것을 바꿀 수가 없다고 하여 오빠가 해가 되는 유형도 있다.’

checks.q_en: At the first hill pass, what did the tiger ask the mother for?
What came down from the sky to help the children?

options: She wanted to see the sunrise
She was afraid of the dark night
She felt the sun was too hot
Her brother asked to shine first

episodes.reference_display: Traditional folk tale, one version retold gently and simplified (versions differ). As told in: 한국민족문화대백과사전 「해와 달이 된 오누이」 (한국학중앙연구원) and 한국민속문학사전 「해와 달이 된 오누이」 (국립민속박물관); 국립국어원 표준국어대사전. Not history.
episodes.notes: REVISED 2026-10-10. Traditional tale: narration describes what happens in the tale, not history. Two authoritative sources now: the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (E0062663; basic version with three siblings) and the National Folk Museum's 한국민속문학사전 entry by 조현설 (topic 6006; summary with two children, whose folk-literature dictionary cites 한국구비문학대계 1-4, 811; 1-5, 308; 2-6, 473; 2-7, 513 as its sources - the 구비문학대계 recordings themselves could not be opened with the tools used, gubi.aks.ac.kr returned nothing). The sesame-oil episode (f4) rests on the Encyclopedia only (the NFM summary does not mention it); claims kept minimal. Differences between sources, stated openly in the facts: Encyclopedia - mother met at successive hill passes with demands rice cake, clothes, arms, legs, torso; children open the door when the tiger says it must nurse the baby; the sun-sister pricks people's eyes with needles. NFM - children see the tiger through a hole in the door and flee by the back door; the sun-sister gives off a strong light. This retelling follows the gentler options where they exist. Softened on purpose: the tiger eating the mother and the baby; the demands for clothes, arms, legs and torso; the axe; the tiger's death on the sorghum stalks (told as 'the end of its tricks'); the needles. Three siblings (삼 남매) in the Encyclopedia vs. two (오누이) in the NFM summary: narration says 'the children' and mentions the crying baby only because the tiger uses it as an excuse. 님 is a gender-neutral respectful suffix; in this retelling the sun is the sister and the moon the brother, so the 'Mr. Sun, Ms. Moon' gloss was removed. Reassurance beats added in scenes 4, 7 and 8. The line '떡 하나 주면 안 잡아먹지' is not used (not in the sources; too scary for young children). Hoya's 'not like me!' is character banter. Stage 5 'Tiger Folktales' is a natural placement, but the language is at Listen level, hence recommended_stage 1.

episodes.title_en: Pansori Tales: Heungbu's Swallow and the Clever Rabbit (Traditional Tales)
episodes.title_ko: 판소리 이야기: 흥부와 놀부, 토끼와 자라
episodes.summary_en: Hoya visits a pansori performance (UNESCO 2003/2008) and hears two traditional stories from its five surviving works: kind Heungbu and the grateful swallow, and the clever rabbit who escapes the Dragon King's palace. This Korean rabbit-and-turtle tale is a different story from Aesop's 'The Tortoise and the Hare'.
learning_goals: Describe pansori: one singer, one drummer with a buk, and chuimsae cheers like 'Eolssigu!'.
Know that five pansori works survive today, including Heungboga and Sugungga, which also exist as old novels.
Retell the main events of Heungbu and Nolbu and of the rabbit and the turtle (jara), and know that this rabbit-and-turtle tale is not Aesop's 'The Tortoise and the Hare'.
Recognize and say 판소리, 북, 추임새, 얼씨구, 제비, 박, 토끼 and 자라.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya takes a seat for pansori! One singer, the sorikkun, tells a long story by singing, speaking and acting. A drummer, the gosu, keeps the rhythm on a barrel drum called a buk.
scenes.illustration: A singer in a white hanbok holding a folding fan, standing on a straw mat; a seated drummer with a round barrel drum beside her; Hoya in the audience.

scenes.narration_en: The drummer shouts cheers called chuimsae, like 'Eolssigu!' and 'Jota!' Long ago there were twelve pansori stories; five are still sung today. UNESCO named pansori a masterpiece in 2003 and added it to its Representative List in 2008. Let's hear two!
scenes.illustration: The drummer mid-shout with one hand raised, the singer opening her fan; five small scroll shapes floating above, two of them glowing.

scenes.narration_en: First, Heungboga, also told as the old novel Heungbu-jeon. Nolbu, the older brother, was greedy. Heungbu, the younger, was poor but kind. One spring, Heungbu found a baby swallow with a broken leg and gently bound it up.
scenes.illustration: A kind man in patched clothes cupping a baby swallow and tying a tiny strip of cloth around its leg outside a humble straw hut.

scenes.narration_en: The next spring, the swallow returned with a gourd seed. Heungbu planted it, and huge gourds grew. When his family sawed them open, out poured money, rice and treasures!
scenes.illustration: Huge round white gourds on a thatched roof; a family sawing one open with a two-person saw as rice and shining treasures spill out; a swallow circling.

scenes.narration_en: Greedy Nolbu wanted treasure too, so he hurt a swallow on purpose. But his gourds brought only trouble! In well-known versions, Nolbu was sorry and became kind, and the brothers lived in peace.
scenes.illustration: Two brothers in hanbok embracing in front of a modest house, one looking ashamed and grateful; a swallow perched on the eaves.

scenes.narration_en: Next, Sugungga, also told as the novel Tokki-jeon. It is a different story from Aesop's race! The Dragon King is sick, and a sage says a rabbit's liver can cure him. A loyal jara, a soft-shelled turtle titled Byeoljubu, volunteers to fetch one.
scenes.illustration: An undersea palace of coral and seaweed; a dragon king resting on a cushion; a small soft-shelled turtle in an official's hat bowing and volunteering.

scenes.narration_en: On land, the turtle tells the rabbit about a high post waiting for him at the sea palace. The rabbit is fooled and follows him down. But at the palace, the king demands his liver! Don't worry: clever Rabbit has a plan.
scenes.illustration: The rabbit arriving wide-eyed in the undersea palace beside the turtle, fish courtiers watching; the king pointing; bubbles everywhere, nothing frightening.

scenes.narration_en: Rabbit thinks fast: 'I left my liver back on land!' The king believes him and sends him home with the turtle. On the shore, Rabbit hops off into the forest. Eolssigu! An early form of this tale is even recorded in the Samguk sagi.
scenes.gloss_en: I left my liver on land.
scenes.illustration: A rabbit bounding happily into a green forest from a sandy shore while the turtle watches from the waves; Hoya in the audience cheering with raised paws.

facts.claim_en: In pansori, one singer (sorikkun) tells a long story by singing, speaking and gesturing, accompanied by a drummer (gosu) who keeps the rhythm on a barrel drum (buk).
facts.claim_ko: 판소리는 한 명의 소리꾼이 고수(북치는 사람)의 장단에 맞추어 창·아니리·너름새를 섞어가며 긴 이야기를 엮어가는 공연이다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 판소리 (Pansori)
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘판소리는 한 명의 소리꾼이 고수(북치는 사람)의 장단에 맞추어 창(소리), 말(아니리), 몸짓(너름새)을 섞어가며 긴 이야기를 엮어가는 것을 말한다.’

sources.title: Pansori epic chant
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘Pansori is a genre of musical storytelling performed by a vocalist and a drummer.’

sources.title: 판소리
sources.quote_or_locator: 정의: ‘한 명의 창자(唱者)가 고수(鼓手)의 북장단에 맞추어 서사적인 이야기를 소리와 아니리로 엮어 발림을 곁들이며 구연하는 전통 공연 예술.’

sources.title: 판소리 (한국민속문학사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전

facts.claim_en: The drummer calls out exclamations such as 'Eolssigu!' and 'Jota!' to lift the performance; these are called chuimsae.
facts.claim_ko: 고수는 “얼씨구”, “좋다” 같은 감탄사로 흥을 돋우는데, 이를 추임새라고 한다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 판소리
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘고수의 반주는 … “얼씨구”, “좋다”, “으이”, “그렇지” 등의 감탄사를 내는데, 이를 추임새라고 한다.’

sources.title: 추임새
sources.publisher: 국립국어원 (National Institute of Korean Language) — 표준국어대사전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘판소리에서, 장단을 짚는 고수(鼓手)가 창(唱)의 사이사이에 흥을 돋우기 위하여 삽입하는 소리. ‘좋지’, ‘얼씨구’, ‘흥’ 따위이다.’

sources.title: 추임새 (한국민속문학사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: 정의: ‘판소리 공연 중에 고수와 청관중이 … ‘얼씨구·좋다·어이·그렇지·잘 헌다·하아’ 등의 감탄사를 발하여 메꾸어 나아가는 공연 행위.’

facts.claim_en: Pansori once had twelve works (madang); five are still performed today: Chunhyangga, Simcheongga, Sugungga, Heungboga and Jeokbyeokga.
facts.claim_ko: 판소리는 한때 열두 마당이 있었으나, 오늘날 춘향가·심청가·수궁가·흥보가·적벽가 다섯 마당이 전승된다.

sources.title: 국가무형유산 판소리
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘판소리 열두 마당이라 하여 … 그 수가 많았다.’ / ‘춘향가, 심청가, 수궁가, 흥보가, 적벽가만이 보다 예술적인 음악으로 가다듬어져 판소리 다섯마당으로 정착되었다.’

sources.title: 판소리
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘판소리는 현재 전승되는 다섯 바탕 외에도 … 『관우희(觀優戱)』에는 … 열두 바탕이 기록되어 있고’

facts.claim_en: Pansori was proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003 and incorporated into the Representative List in 2008.
facts.claim_ko: 판소리는 2003년 유네스코 걸작으로 선정되고 2008년 인류무형문화유산 대표목록에 통합 등재되었다.

sources.title: Pansori epic chant
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘Inscribed in 2008 (3.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (originally proclaimed in 2003)’

sources.title: 판소리
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘2003년에는 판소리가 유네스코 인류 무형 문화유산에 등재되었다.’

facts.claim_en: Heungboga is one of the five pansori works; the same story exists as the late-Joseon novel Heungbu-jeon (author and date unknown), in which the greedy older brother Nolbu and the poor, kind younger brother Heungbu appear, and Heungbu binds the broken leg of a fallen baby swallow.
facts.claim_ko: 흥보가는 판소리 다섯 마당의 하나이며, 같은 이야기가 작자·연대 미상의 조선 후기 소설 「흥부전」으로도 전한다. 욕심 많은 형 놀부와 가난하고 착한 아우 흥부가 등장하고, 흥부는 떨어져 다리가 부러진 새끼 제비의 다리를 매어 준다.

sources.title: 흥보가
sources.quote_or_locator: 정의: ‘판소리 다섯마당 가운데 하나.’ / ‘가난하고 착한 아우 흥보는 부러진 제비다리를 고쳐주고’

sources.title: 흥부전
sources.quote_or_locator: ‘작자·연대 미상의 고전소설.’ ‘조선 후기 판소리계 소설로’ / ‘악하고 사나운 형 놀부와 순하고 착한 아우 흥부가 살았는데’ / ‘새끼 한 마리가 땅에 떨어져 다리가 부러졌다. 흥부가 새끼 제비를 불쌍히 여겨 그 다리를 매어 주니’

sources.title: 놀보박타령 (한국민속문학사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quote_or_locator: 내용: ‘<놀보박타령>은 놀보가 자신의 욕심을 못 이겨 박을 타다 결국 박 속에서 등장한 군상들에 의해 몰락하기에 이른다는 내용’ / ‘놀보의 끝없는 물욕’ (supports calling Nolbu greedy)

facts.claim_en: In the story, the swallow returns the next spring with a gourd seed; Heungbu plants it, grows large gourds, and when they are sawn open, money, rice and treasures pour out.
facts.claim_ko: 이듬해 봄 제비가 박씨를 물어다 주고, 흥부가 심어 큰 박을 타자 돈과 쌀, 금은보화가 나온다.

sources.title: 흥부전

facts.claim_en: In the story, Nolbu deliberately hurts a swallow and his gourds release only harmful things and ruin him. Endings differ between versions: in the basic plot of the novel Heungbu-jeon (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture) and in well-known sung versions of Heungboga (the Park Bong-sul and Jeong Gwang-su texts described by the National Folk Museum's folk-literature dictionary), Nolbu repents and the brothers are reconciled.

facts.claim_en: Sugungga is one of the five pansori works; the same story exists as the late-Joseon novel Tokki-jeon (also called Byeoljubu-jeon). In it the Dragon King falls ill, a sage (dosa) says a rabbit's liver will cure him, and the jara (soft-shelled turtle) called Byeoljubu volunteers to go to land. Byeoljubu (鼈主簿) is a title for the turtle (鼈 'soft-shelled turtle' + 主簿, an old official title), not a personal name.
facts.claim_ko: 수궁가는 판소리 다섯 마당의 하나이며, 같은 이야기가 조선 후기 소설 「토끼전」(「별주부전」)으로도 전한다. 용왕이 병들자 도사가 토끼의 간을 먹으면 낫는다고 하고, 별주부(鼈主簿) 자라가 자원하여 육지로 간다. ‘별주부’는 자라에게 붙은 관직 이름(鼈 자라 + 主簿)으로 사람 이름이 아니다.

facts.claim_en: In the story, the turtle lures the rabbit by promising a high official post at the undersea palace; the rabbit is fooled and follows him to the Dragon King's palace, where the king demands his liver.

facts.claim_en: In the story, the rabbit claims he left his liver on land; the king sends him back with the turtle, and on land the rabbit escapes into the forest.

facts.claim_en: Korea's rabbit-and-turtle tale (Sugungga / Tokki-jeon) is a different story from Aesop's fable of the hare and the tortoise (titled 'The Hare and the Tortoise' in the Townsend translation cited here, and also known as 'The Tortoise and the Hare'): in Aesop's fable a hare and a tortoise run a race, while in the Korean tale a turtle is sent to bring a rabbit's liver to the sick Dragon King.
facts.claim_ko: 한국의 토끼와 자라 이야기(수궁가·토끼전)는 토끼와 거북이 달리기를 하는 이솝 우화 「토끼와 거북이」와 다른 이야기이다. 한국 이야기에서는 병든 용왕을 위해 자라가 토끼의 간을 구하러 육지로 간다.

episodes.reference_display: Traditional tales (retold gently). Korea's rabbit-and-turtle tale (Sugungga / Tokki-jeon) is a different story from Aesop's 'The Tortoise and the Hare'. Sources: 국가유산청 국가유산포털(판소리·인류무형유산 목록); UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage; 한국민족문화대백과사전; 한국민속대백과사전(국립민속박물관); 국립국어원 표준국어대사전
episodes.notes: REVISED 2026-10-10. Traditional stories: narration describes the tales' content (basic plot per the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture and the National Folk Museum's folk-literature dictionary), not history. Names: the pansori work is 흥보가 (Heungbo/Nolbo) and the novel is 흥부전 (Heungbu/Nolbu); narration uses Heungbu/Nolbu. Ending: the repentance/reconciliation is in the basic plot of the novel Heungbu-jeon (E0066012) AND in the Park Bong-sul and Jeong Gwang-su sung texts (한국민속문학사전 '놀보박타령'); the Encyclopedia's Heungboga entry itself says only that Nolbo is ruined; endings differ (e.g. the 경판본 version ends differently; 신재효's text is described as similar to Jeong Gwang-su's), so narration says 'In well-known versions'. Softened on purpose: Heungbu being beaten and his paid stand-in beatings (매품팔이); Nolbu breaking the swallow's leg is shown only as 'hurt a swallow on purpose'; harmful things from Nolbu's gourds not detailed. Rabbit tale: 'liver' kept because the plot needs it, with a reassurance line right after; the turtle's fate (dies on land or returns empty-handed; in some versions the rabbit's droppings cure the king) is left out. 별주부 (鼈主簿) is the turtle's title, not a name; the 도사 is a sage (道士: one who cultivates the Way). The Korean tale is explicitly distinguished from Aesop's race (summary, scene 6, reference_display, f11). 구토지설: 한국민속문학사전 '수궁가' says Sugungga's frame is the 구토지설 told by Seon Do-hae to Kim Chun-chu and recorded in the Samguk sagi's biographies; the Encyclopedia ('토끼전') names the 구토 tale in the Kim Yu-sin biography as a documented example - narration says only 'an early form is recorded in the Samguk sagi'. Both sources note the older Indian Buddhist (Jataka) roots; not used. 추임새 is now taught in scene 2 and added to vocab (형제 dropped from vocab; it remains the scene 5 Korean word). Combined in one episode to keep the cluster at 6; each could become its own episode. Theme 'crafts' because the app files performing arts under Play & Crafts. FINAL PASS (3rd check, 2026-10-10): scene 2 now says UNESCO named pansori a masterpiece in 2003 and added it to the Representative List in 2008 (UNESCO page: inscribed 2008, originally proclaimed 2003). f11 now gives the Aesop title as in the cited Townsend text ('The Hare and the Tortoise', also known as 'The Tortoise and the Hare'). 'Greedy' for Nolbu rests on the NFM 놀보박타령 entry, which was added to f5.

verification.notes: Third independent pass over 6 episodes / 61 facts / 161 source entries (70 unique URLs). Every URL was re-fetched with my own scripts (UNESCO pages via Wayback copies; heritage.go.kr descriptions via the portal ajax html and khs.go.kr open API; folkency via its JSON API) and each quote or locator was machine-matched to the page text; the few non-matching strings were checked by hand (portal metadata fields, hanja or footnote punctuation, label text). Corrections: (1) pansori scene 2 now gives both UNESCO steps (2003 masterpiece proclamation, 2008 Representative List); (2) pansori f11 states the Aesop title as in the cited Townsend text and the common alternate title; (3) added sources: NFM 놀보박타령 for 'greedy' (f5), 표준국어대사전 타다 for 'sawed' (f6), 한국민족문화대백과사전 선도해 for the Samguk sagi tale (f12); (4) Seollal f9/f10 designation-date locators now cite the KHS open API field. No other change. See seasons-tales.signoff.md.
